title.en: Coins and trade in history (additional, not in the textbook)

text.en:
A trader long ago carried salt from the coast to a faraway town. There he swapped it for cloth, but he could not carry much cloth back.
"If only I had small coins that everyone accepts," he sighed, "I could take home whatever I need."

Before coins, people used barter. This was difficult because both sides had to want what the other had. Later people used shells, grain and metal pieces as money.
Some of the earliest Indian coins were punch-marked coins of silver, made about 2500 years ago. Kings and traders issued coins, and later rulers such as the Guptas issued fine gold coins. Coins helped trade, tax collection and payment of workers.
Land and sea routes carried goods such as spices, cotton, silk and pearls to and from other lands. Guilds of traders and craftspeople helped organise this trade. Coins also teach historians about the rulers and times.
Barter is exchanging goods for goods. It is difficult.
Coins were easier. Early Indian coins were punch-marked silver coins.
Traders carried spices, cotton and pearls along land and sea routes.
Coins also help historians learn about rulers and times.

problem.en: How did coins make trade easier than barter?

text.en: In barter both sides must want each other's goods.
Coins are accepted by everyone, so a seller can take coins and buy later.
So coins make trade simple and quick.

why.en: They also make tax payments easy.

prompt.en: A friend says coins are just old metal with no use for history. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Coins show rulers' names, pictures and the metals they used.
They help historians date events and learn about trade.

points.en: Barter was replaced by money and coins.
Early Indian coins were punch-marked silver coins.
Coins and routes helped trade and teach history.
